intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene (605363) on chromosome 2q31.

checks.claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous variants were identified in five families (Families A, B, D, E and F), whereas compound heterozygous variants were found in Family C (Table 2).
checks.explanation: The paper presents bi-allelic GAD1 variants as a new cause of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. DEE89 is the standard name for this disorder.

checks.claim: The GAD1 gene is located on chromosome 2q31.
checks.evidence_quote: In vertebrates, GAD exists in two isoforms, GAD67 and GAD65, encoded by two independent genes GAD1 and GAD2, respectively.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature; not stated in paper but accepted.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive disorder. Seizures begin in early infancy, and patients have hypotonia and severe developmental delay. Some patients also have variable non-CNS features, such as skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features and cleft palate (Neuray et al., 2020). Chatron et al. (2020) described the disorder as a neonatal-onset syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. In their patients, epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures began in the first 2 months of life and were accompanied by profound psychomotor delay. Some patients also had cleft palate, joint contractures, pes equinovarus or omphalocele.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients with a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy from 6 unrelated consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish, Iranian and Brazilian origin. Seizures began in the first 2 months of life in all patients, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. Early EEG showed suppression-burst, burst attenuation or hypsarrhythmia. Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus, 7 had cleft palate and 2 had omphalocele. All living patients had profound psychomotor delay, and 4 patients died before 4 years of age.

paragraphs.text: Family A of Chatron et al. (2020) had 2 affected sibs, a boy and a girl, born to Algerian first-cousin parents. Both had cleft soft palate. By 5 months of age the boy had developmental regression, axial hypotonia and hypsarrhythmia. At 6 years he had spastic tetraparesis and no speech. His sister had spasms from 2 days of age, and her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern. Her seizures were controlled by 3 months of age with levetiracetam and vigabatrin, but she had severe developmental delay with axial hypotonia.

paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients (3 male, 3 female) from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian and Turkish ancestry. Four of the families were consanguineous. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures. Some patients also had epileptic spasms, focal non-motor seizures or bilateral motor seizures. Seizures were controlled with medication in 3 patients and were drug-resistant in the other 3. At seizure onset, EEG showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Brain MRI was normal in 4 patients. Of the other 2, 1 had slight ventricular enlargement and 1 had moderate global atrophy.

paragraphs.text: All 6 patients of Neuray et al. (2020) had severe developmental delay. Most never developed speech or non-verbal communication. Intellectual disability was severe in 5 patients and moderate in 1. Five patients had reduced muscle strength or tone. Of these, 4 lacked head control or could not sit or crawl, and 2 depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Four patients had mild facial dysmorphism, and 1 had cleft palate. Other features occurred without a common pattern: hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs, congenital hip dislocation, high myopia and hearing impairment. Metabolic workups were normal. Three of the 6 patients became seizure-free, yet all had severe intellectual disability, so cognitive development did not improve even when seizures were controlled. The authors hypothesized that GAD1 variants affect development independently of seizure control.
